subject: Biologi
title: What is life? Cells and organisation
sourceSummary: What characterises living organisms and how the cell is life's smallest building block. You also practise the difference between plant cells and animal cells, and how cells build up tissues and organs.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a characteristic that ALL living organisms have?
questions.opener: Think about what a cat, a pine tree and a bacterium actually have in common.
questions.explanation: All living organisms reproduce, grow, respire, take up nutrients and react to their surroundings. Being able to walk or having a heart only applies to certain animals — a pine tree has neither legs nor a heart but is still alive.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the cell being life's smallest building block?
questions.opener: Think about what the smallest thing is that can live entirely on its own.
choices: The cell is the smallest part that can live and carry out the functions of life
The cell is the smallest part you can see with the naked eye
The cell is the smallest part of a skeleton
The cell is the smallest molecule in the body
questions.explanation: A cell can take up nutrients, get rid of waste and divide — it is alive. Molecules are indeed smaller, but a single molecule is not alive; it can only be part of something living.

questions.prompt: Which cell part is found in a plant cell but missing from an animal cell?
questions.opener: Think about why a flower stalk can stand upright and why the leaves are green.
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis — they are found only in plants, which also have a cell wall. The nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm are found in both cell types, so they do not work as a difference.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the nucleus?
questions.opener: Somewhere in the cell is the blueprint for how everything should work.
choices: It contains the genetic material and controls the cell's work
It lets substances in and out of the cell
It gives the cell its green colour
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains the DNA, the genetic material, which determines what the cell should do. A common mistake is to confuse the nucleus with the cell membrane — but it is the membrane, not the nucleus, that handles transport in and out.

questions.prompt: What is formed when many cells of the same kind sit together and do the same job?
questions.opener: It is the level right above the cell.
questions.explanation: Identical cells together form a tissue, for example muscle tissue. An organ, such as the stomach, is the next level and consists of several different tissues together.

questions.prompt: Why do you need a microscope to study cells?
questions.opener: Think about how big a cell is compared with what you can see without any aid.
choices: Because cells only exist in water
Because cells are dangerous to touch
Because most cells are far too small to see with the naked eye
questions.explanation: Most cells are only a few hundredths of a millimetre in size, so the eye cannot make them out — the microscope magnifies the image many times over. The idea that cells would move too fast is not correct; the problem is size, not speed.

questions.prompt: Describe how the body is built up from cell to organ system. Use the stomach as an example.
questions.opener: Go through four levels in order: cell, tissue, organ, organ system.
questions.answer: Cells of the same kind form a tissue, several tissues build up the organ called the stomach, and the stomach works together with the mouth, the oesophagus and the intestines in the digestive system.
steps: The cell is the smallest living building block, for example a muscle cell in the wall of the stomach.
Many identical cells together form a tissue, here muscle tissue.
Several different tissues build up an organ — the stomach.
The stomach works together with the oesophagus and the intestines and forms the digestive system, an organ system.

questions.prompt: What characterises everything living, and what parts does a cell have?
questions.opener: First name the characteristics of life, then the cell parts — and which ones are found only in plants.
questions.answer: Characteristics of life: grows and develops · takes up nutrients · respires and converts energy · gets rid of waste · reacts to its surroundings · reproduces · is built up of cells · Cell parts in both plant and animal: nucleus (genetic material, controls the cell) · cell membrane (regulates what goes in and out) · cytoplasm (jelly-like fluid where the parts sit) · mitochondria (release energy from nutrients) · Only in plant cells: cell wall (gives structure) · chloroplasts (photosynthesis, green chlorophyll) · large vacuole (water storage) · Levels in the body: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism · A microscope is needed because cells are too small for the naked eye.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of life?
questions.opener: Think about a pine tree — it cannot move at all, yet it is still alive.
choices: Can travel through space under its own power
questions.explanation: Travelling through space under its own power is not a characteristic of life — it describes a rocket rather than a living thing. Plants, which are rooted in place, are a good example that living organisms don't need to be able to move.

questions.prompt: What is the jelly-like fluid inside the cell called, where the other parts sit?
questions.opener: Think about what fills the rest of the cell between the nucleus and the membrane.
questions.explanation: The cytoplasm is the jelly-like fluid surrounding the cell's other parts, such as the nucleus and the mitochondria. The cell wall exists only in plants, and the cell membrane is the cell's outer boundary.

questions.prompt: Which cell part releases energy from nutrients?
questions.opener: This cell part is sometimes called "the powerhouse of the cell".
questions.explanation: Mitochondria break down nutrients using oxygen and release energy the cell can use. The nucleus instead controls the cell's work through its genetic material.

questions.prompt: Which cell part gives plant cells their structure and fixed shape?
questions.opener: Think about why a plant cell keeps its shape even without a skeleton.
questions.explanation: The cell wall is a hard, rigid layer outside the cell membrane that gives plant cells their structure. Animal cells lack a cell wall, which is one of the clearest differences between plant and animal cells.

questions.prompt: What is it called when several different tissues work together and form a unit, such as the heart?
questions.opener: It's the level right above tissue.
questions.explanation: An organ, such as the heart, is built up of several different tissues working together, for example muscle tissue and nerve tissue. An organism is instead the next level up, a whole living individual.

questions.prompt: Which of these would you need a microscope to see clearly?
questions.opener: Think about which option is far too small for the naked eye.
questions.explanation: A cell nucleus is only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size and can only be seen with a microscope. Ants, leaves and dogs can all be seen with the naked eye, even if less clearly in detail.

questions.prompt: Describe how the body is built up from cell to organ system. Use the heart as an example.
questions.opener: Go through the same four levels as before: cell, tissue, organ, organ system — but with the heart.
questions.answer: Cells of the same kind form a tissue, several tissues build up the organ called the heart, and the heart works together with the blood vessels in the circulatory system, which is an organ system.
steps: The cell is the smallest living building block, for example a heart muscle cell.
Many identical cells together form a tissue, here heart muscle tissue.
Several different tissues build up an organ — the heart.
The heart works together with the blood vessels and forms the circulatory system, an organ system.
